content: A study published in the May 2006 edition of the American Journal of Hypertension compared the effectiveness of home blood pressure monitoring and 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring in guiding antihypertensive treatment. The findings demonstrated that home blood pressure monitoring is as accurate as 24-hour ambulatory monitoring in determining arterial pressure levels. Researchers from the University of Turku in Finland conducted the study on 98 patients with untreated hypertension. They compared patients using a home arterial pressure device with those wearing a 24-hour ambulatory monitor. Dr. Niiranen, one of the researchers, stated, Home blood pressure measurement can be used effectively for guiding antihypertensive treatment. Dr. Stergiou added that home monitoring of arterial pressure is more convenient and also less costly than ambulatory blood pressure monitoring. In May 2007, another clinical study published in the American Journal of Hypertension evaluated the accuracy of three different methods of measuring arterial pressure in assessing cardiovascular health. The study aimed to compare home blood pressure monitoring (HBP), 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABP), and office-based arterial pressure readings (OBP). These measurements were compared to the left ventricular mass index (LVMI), which was calculated using echocardiography. LVMI serves as an indicator of cardiovascular organ damage and reflects arterial pressure. Researchers at Columbia University Medical Center in New York found that home blood pressure monitoring over a 10-week period was a significant independent predictor of LVMI, even after adjusting for age, sex, and body mass index (BMI). They concluded that home monitoring over time is a better indicator of cardiovascular health than ambulatory readings or office-based measurements. The value of home monitoring increases with the number of measurements taken over time. In June 2007, AM News, a newspaper for American physicians, published a study highlighting the unreliability of arterial pressure readings taken in a doctor’s office. The American Medical Association newspaper quoted Professor Norman Kaplan from the University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, who stated, Of all the procedures done in a doctor’s office, measurement of blood pressure is usually the least well performed but has the most important implications for the care of the patient. The article explained that office-based arterial pressure readings can be falsely elevated or lowered due to the presence of a doctor or clinician, a phenomenon known as white coat hypertension. The American Heart Association website notes, You may have what’s called ‘white coat hypertension’; that means your blood pressure goes up when you’re at the doctor’s office. Monitoring at home will help you measure your true blood pressure and can provide your doctor with a log of blood pressure measurements over time. This is helpful in diagnosing and preventing potential health problems. The use of home arterial pressure monitoring devices is increasingly accompanied by arterial pressure charting software. These tools provide printouts for physicians and reminders for patients on how often to check their blood pressure. For home blood pressure readings to be accurate, they must be taken consistently and correctly. The National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute offers guidelines to ensure accurate readings. These include avoiding coffee or smoking 30 minutes before the measurement, sitting for five minutes with your back supported and feet flat on the ground, resting your arm at heart level, wearing short sleeves to expose your arm, and emptying your bladder before taking the reading.
